speaker_role: current admissions officer (Boston University, unnamed in transcript)
commercial_incentive: Clip is presented as promotional content ('brought to you by') for the Massachusetts School of Law at Andover, though the substantive content itself is not selling a service to viewers
key_insights: Debunks the 'more is better' myth: piling on 15-20 activities does not strengthen an application; officers prefer depth and demonstrated commitment to one or two pursuits (illustrated via a ballet-dancer analogy).

Holistic review is explicitly not formula- or SAT-driven; teacher and counselor recommendations are used to assess 'fit' and classroom behaviors invisible elsewhere (preparedness, participation, resilience when struggling).
Initial review starts from the high school transcript; competitive applicants in the cited year had roughly an A average.
Grades alone are insufficient -- curriculum rigor (honors/AP courses) is weighted heavily because AP courses demonstrate capacity to handle college-level work.
With a very large applicant pool relative to class size, rigor and substantive, specific recommendations are the primary tools used to narrow candidates and identify 'red flags.'
specific_numbers_or_facts: Boston University speaker: the university received 'over fifty-four thousand' applications for a freshman class of about 3,600 in the cited year.
notable_or_distinctive: A concise, on-the-record statement from a BU admissions officer explicitly naming and debunking the 'more activities is better' myth using a concrete personal analogy (a ballet dancer niece).
reliability_notes: Very short (4-minute) promotional excerpt from an older video (published ~11 years ago per manifest), so cited figures are dated; content overlaps substantially with quality-over-quantity and curriculum-rigor themes covered more extensively elsewhere in this batch (e.g., the Becky Sabky/Dartmouth talk).
